headline: Anthropic Investors Discover Money Before Company Discovers Profits
subheadline: Early backers are already rich on paper—which is the only place their returns actually exist.
source_headline: What some of Anthropic's backers are reportedly worth before its IPO
body_html:
Anthropic's early investors are reportedly sitting on major paper returns ahead of the AI lab's expected initial public offering, according to recent reporting. This is the part of the startup cycle where venture capitalists and their limited partners gather around the proverbial fireplace to discuss the imaginary wealth they've accumulated—which is to say, the valuations assigned by later-stage investors who are themselves betting the company will somehow justify a price tag that would make a Fortune 50 company blush. The fact that this story exists at all, and that it warrants coverage, tells you everything you need to know about the current state of financial journalism.

Anthropic is an AI safety and research company—which is venture-speak for "we make large language models and pray they don't become sentient or, alternatively, that they become sentient enough to justify our Series E." The company has raised substantial capital from blue-chip investors and is widely expected to pursue a public exit, which means its backers are now engaged in the sacred ritual of watching their spreadsheets calculate wealth that may or may not survive contact with actual financial markets. No one reporting on these paper returns seems particularly interested in asking the obvious follow-up question: at what multiple of revenue are we pricing this company, and what happens when the IPO roadshow requires management to explain how they'll generate enough actual cash to justify it?

This is not the first time venture investors have celebrated phantom riches before an exit event, nor will it be the last. The pattern is as old as the asset class itself: early-stage capital compounds beautifully through successive rounds of late-stage hype-inflation, each new investor paying a higher price than the last, each one betting that the next guy will pay even more. Anthropic's backers are not pioneering this strategy; they are executing a playbook that worked spectacularly in 2020, worked reasonably in 2021, worked less well in 2022, and is now attempting a comeback in an environment where the cost of capital has actually risen and public market multiples have compressed. The fact that people are writing celebration pieces about unrealized gains suggests that no one has learned anything.

The subtext of every "major paper returns" story is a bet that the IPO window will remain open, that public market investors will be as credulous as late-stage VCs have been, and that the company's business fundamentals—whatever those are—won't become a focal point of due diligence. Anthropic is a genuinely capable research organization, but capability and unit economics are not the same thing, and venture investors have spent two decades confusing the two. The company's backers are rich in theory; they will discover whether they're rich in practice the moment a bank of underwriters has to explain to institutional investors why this particular startup deserves a $10+ billion market capitalization.

What happens when paper returns meet public market scrutiny? The answer is usually some combination of a lower-than-expected IPO price, post-IPO volatility, and lock-up period hangovers that remind everyone why late-stage venture returns are so lumpy. Anthropic's investors may indeed be sitting on major multiples—that part is probably true, statistically speaking—but multiples are not cash, and cash is not a business model. The gap between the two is where most venture wealth ultimately vanishes.

We are not questioning Anthropic's talent or technology; we are questioning whether the financial press has developed any muscle memory for skepticism whatsoever. A story celebrating investor paper returns ahead of an exit event is not news—it is marketing, filed under the business section to make it sound like analysis. The real story would be an honest accounting of what revenue multiple we're paying, and what could possibly justify it. Until then, these unrealized gains are just very expensive air.
glossary_definition: Wealth that exists exclusively in spreadsheets and term sheets until the moment an investor tries to actually spend it.
